summary: The Next Window is our answer to the Space Mission Design Game challenge: a web game (English and Spanish) for students aged 12 and up, with two ways into the same Mars mission. In the Design Table, one to four players design a crew expedition to Gale Crater from the objective down: instruments, power, oxygen, data link, shelter, trip and rocket, under live limits of mass, power, data, budget, time and radiation dose. Each player takes a role with their own goal; when the goals clash, the team votes. The design is then simulated with real events (dust storms, solar storms, the solar conjunction) and scored out of 1000, with a report that explains why it worked or failed and compares it with NASA's own reference plan (Mars DRA 5.0). In the 3D adventure, the player lives that mission from the inside, in a base built to their design: a command room that asks for new decisions after each operation, six playable missions (panels before a solar storm, a MOXIE-like oxygen plant, an iron meteorite, an engine test, the solar-conjunction blackout, and the ascent, docking and Hohmann burn home) and a final report. Every number and photo comes from NASA data, stamped as archive data (◌), calculation (≈) or game assumption (△), with its source one tap away.
details:
What it does. One Mars mission, played two ways: the Design Table and the 3D adventure.

The Design Table (1–4 players) covers the full mission-design loop. Define the objective first: search for life, water and air to stay, or weather and radiation; each sets its own requirements (sols of science, Gbit returned to Earth) and key instruments. Design the expedition in eight decisions: objective, instruments (SAM, SHERLOC, RIMFAX, MOXIE, MEDA, RAD), power, oxygen, data link (including an orbiter relay), shelter, trip type and rocket (SLS Block 1, 1B or 2 × number of launches). Every choice moves the live dashboard: mass vs. what the rockets can lift, power demand vs. supply, data made vs. what fits through the link, budget in credits, days away and radiation dose. A one-minute guided tour by Vale, the mission director, shows first-time players how the table works.

Review before launch: eight green/yellow/red checks ("Does it fit in the rocket?", "Is there enough power, with margin?", "Does the dose stay under the limit?"...), with a one-tap fix for each red light. Collaborate: up to four designers with roles — mission director (goal, trip, rocket), science (instruments), engineering (power, oxygen), health and comms (link, shelter). Each role has its own target; when the targets clash, each player may propose one change and the team votes.

Simulate and evaluate: the mission runs on real orbits with dust storms, solar storms and the solar conjunction, then a report scores science, crew safety, efficiency and budget (out of 1000), explains every event and the decision and role behind it, and compares the design with NASA's Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0. Replay and compare: four levels (Cadet, Engineer, Mission chief, and a free sandbox), a share code for every design and a mission board on the device. "Live this mission" carries the design into the 3D adventure: the base shows what the player chose (a fission reactor behind its berm, solar blankets, a second oxygen plant, oxygen tanks from Earth, a laser terminal), each labeled "your design".

The 3D adventure lets the player live the mission from the inside, as Kofi, the engineer of a four-person crew. A storm destroys the 25 t of oxygen in the ascent ship and the next window home opens in 532 sols. In the command room, the player sets the base's power source, oxygen plant and antenna and sees what each changes (launch mass and SLS rockets needed, power with and without dust, Mbit per sol with Earth, spare sols). After each mission a new decision arrives — for example, a dust storm leaves little power: the plant, the greenhouse or the antenna?

Six playable missions, each a real operation: clean dust off panels before a solar storm (radiation data from Curiosity's RAD); run MOXIE-like oxygen production through a Phobos eclipse; use a ChemCam-like laser to confirm iron meteorites; test-fire the methane–oxygen engines; keep the base alive during the solar-conjunction blackout; and fly the ascent, dock with the return ship and time the Hohmann transfer burn ("aim where Earth will be"). Crew morale is a resource too, and a final report shows how every decision shaped safety, science, crew and margin. Optional: a rover expedition to three real Curiosity sites, a greenhouse with real Veggie data, and the "Earth Jukebox", which turns NASA Earth visualizations into music.

How it works. React 18 + TypeScript + three.js / React Three Fiber, built with Vite, 1,800+ automated tests. All models are procedural (built in code). The Design Table and the missions run on deterministic, seeded simulations; masses, oxygen and propellant needs come from NASA's DRA 5.0, and every number carries a stamp (◌ archive, ≈ calculation, △ assumption). Live data (NOAA SWPC X-rays, NASA POWER weather) is used when available, with saved copies offline. A built-in glossary explains hard words (μGy, sol, Hohmann...) on hover or tap. Accessibility: large high-contrast text, a reduced-motion mode, keyboard, mouse and touch controls, and labels for screen readers.

Benefits and goals. It turns mission design into something a 12-year-old can feel: trade-offs are not abstract, they decide whether the crew gets home. A class can split into teams of four at the Design Table, compare designs with share codes, and then live the mission in 3D. We want students to learn how real missions are planned with limited resources, and to read and trust NASA data. Next: online team play, more scenarios (the Moon, other launch windows) and a Part 2 (the next crew arrives at the base CHISPA kept).

Tools. TypeScript, React, three.js, React Three Fiber, drei, postprocessing, zustand, Vite, Vitest, Puppeteer (automated play-testing), Cloudflare Workers (hosting), ElevenLabs (character voices), Claude (AI coding assistant).
